A2.text:
Kamran's sister, Lala, has a graduation ceremony today at four o'clock. Kamran is driving his mother there. It is half past two, so they have a lot of time.

But Kamran's mother is a back seat driver. “Slow down! Go left! Don't overtake that bus!” she says again and again.

At three o'clock, it is rush hour. There is a big traffic jam on the main road. Nobody can move. Drivers honk, but it does not help. Even the cars in the fast lane are not moving.

“Take a detour,” his mother says. “Go through the small streets.”

Kamran turns into a small street. But after five minutes, they hit a roadblock. Workers are fixing the road, and a sign says “Closed”.

Now it is twenty past three. Kamran's mother looks at the map on her phone. “The metro station is very close,” she says. “Park the car. Let's go!”

They walk quickly to the station. The fare is cheap, and the train comes in two minutes. Kamran usually drives on his commute, so he has not been on the metro for years.

They arrive at the university at ten to four. Lala is waiting at the door.

“How was the drive?” she asks.

Kamran's mother smiles. “Great. Next time, I am the driver.”

options: By car, on the main road

options: She is joking that she has better ideas

questions.why: Her metro idea worked, so she makes a happy joke.

B1.text:
Kamran had promised his sister Lala that he would bring their mother to her graduation ceremony at four o'clock. He left home at half past two, sure that ninety minutes was more than enough to cross Baku.

Unfortunately, his mother was a classic back seat driver. Before they had even left the street, she was giving instructions. “Don't overtake him, he looks dangerous. Why are you in this lane? You're too close to that Prius!”

By three o'clock they had joined the rush hour on Tbilisi Avenue, and soon they were stuck in a traffic jam that stretched to the horizon. Drivers honked as if the noise could push the cars forward. Even the people in the fast lane were sitting still, reading their phones.

“Take a detour through the old streets behind the market,” his mother said.

Kamran didn't want to admit it was a good idea, so he waited a full minute before turning. The narrow streets were moving nicely — until they hit a roadblock. A team of workers was digging up the road, and a fence covered the whole street.

It was now twenty past three. Kamran was beginning to sweat.

His mother was already studying the map on her phone. “The metro is three hundred metres away. Leave the car here. We'll walk.”

They hurried past slow pedestrians, paid the fare and jumped onto a train just as the doors were closing. Kamran had driven on his daily commute for so long that he had forgotten how quick the metro could be. Twelve minutes later, they were climbing the steps towards the university.

They reached the hall at ten to four. Lala ran out to hug them. “How was the traffic?” she asked.

“Terrible,” said their mother. “Fortunately, your brother had me.”

Kamran opened his mouth to argue, then closed it again. She was right, and they both knew it.

questions.q: What is the main point of the story?
options: The annoying back seat driver actually saves the day
questions.why: His mother's metro plan gets them there on time.

How long did the metro journey take?

options: They found the road closed and could not continue

options: He is too tired to speak
He knows his mother is right

B2.text:
Kamran had sworn on everything he owned that he would deliver their mother to Lala's graduation ceremony by four o'clock. He set off at half past two with the confidence of a man who had driven in Baku for a decade and believed he understood its moods.

He had not, however, factored in his passenger. His mother was a back seat driver of near-professional standard, and she was in excellent form. “Don't overtake him — look at his tyres. Why are you hugging the kerb? Indicate! Nobody will know what you're doing!”

By three, they had merged into the rush hour on Tbilisi Avenue and were swallowed by a traffic jam so complete it seemed architectural. Drivers honked in long, furious bursts, as though volume could dissolve metal. Even the cars in the fast lane were frozen, their owners scrolling patiently through their phones.

“Take a detour behind the Yashil Bazaar,” his mother advised. “The old streets will be empty.”

Since admitting she was right would set a dangerous precedent, Kamran waited a full minute before turning, purely as a matter of principle. Annoyingly, the lanes were clear — right up to the moment they hit a roadblock: a crew in orange vests digging a trench across the entire street, behind a fence that left no room even for a motorbike.

It was twenty past three. A bead of sweat made its way down Kamran's neck.

His mother had already zoomed in on the map. “Metro, three hundred metres. Leave the car. We walk.”

They wove between strolling pedestrians, paid the fare and slipped through the closing doors of a train with seconds to spare. Kamran's daily commute was a fixed ritual of radio, coffee and congestion; he had genuinely forgotten that underground the city moved at a completely different speed. Twelve minutes later they were climbing the steps towards the university, his mother barely out of breath.

They walked into the hall at ten to four. Lala threw her arms around them. “How was the drive?”

“A disaster,” their mother said serenely. “Luckily, your brother brought his navigator.”

Kamran drew breath to object, considered the evidence and, for once in his life, said nothing at all.

questions.q: What is the main irony of the story?
options: Kamran is late because of the metro
The passenger Kamran finds annoying turns out to have the best plan
questions.why: His mother's advice gets them there on time.

questions.q: Why did Kamran wait a minute before taking the detour?
options: He did not know the way
He didn't want to admit his mother was right
questions.why: “Admitting she was right would set a dangerous precedent.”
